en: The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Four Dharmas,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan by Imperial Decree.
I take refuge in the Buddha Vairocana, the ocean of great wisdom.
Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of five hundred bhikṣus and eight thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas—all of whom were clad in the firm armor of great and vast vows—as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devaputras from the realms of desire and form, who paid homage to the Tathāgata and listened to receive the essentials of the Dharma.
At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī held a precious parasol, ten yojanas in width, covering the Tathāgata from above.

Then there was a deva from Tuṣita Heaven named Śubhavijaya, who had already attained non-retrogression regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; he was present in this assembly with his retinue and addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Venerable One!..."
"Is making offerings to the Tathāgata still not enough?
Mañjuśrī replied, "What do you think?
Does the ocean ever become satiated by receiving the many rivers?"
The deva replied, “No. Mañjuśrī said:
“O Son of Heaven!
The great ocean is deep and vast, without limit or boundary;
the myriad streams flow toward it as their source, yet it never overflows nor ceases to receive them.”
"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva seeks omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and makes offerings to the Tathāgata, it is likewise such that they never grow weary or satisfied.
The deva further requested, saying:
"When making offerings to the Buddha, what should one do?"
Mañjuśrī replied: "One should do so through four matters:
first, for the sake of sarvajñā (all-knowledge);..."
Second, for the sake of delivering all sentient beings;
third, for the sake of ensuring that the lineage of the Three Jewels is never interrupted;
fourth, for the sake of encompassing the meritorious adornments of all Buddha-fields.
"These are the four matters by which a bodhisattva makes offerings to the Tathāgata.
The deva further requested, saying:
"Excellent, O Venerable One!"
A Bodhisattva should always be without stinginess regarding the Dharma.

Just as you formerly expounded the Bodhisattva path through four Dharma gates for the Brahma King Śikhin and his retinue, we pray that you will once again proclaim this meaning for us and all those gathered here.
Mañjuśrī said: “Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon it well!”
I shall explain this for you.
"O Son of Heaven!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should give rise to four kinds of resolute intention."
What are the four? They are:
gathering the minds of all sentient beings;
and bringing the minds of all sentient beings to maturity.
The mind that gathers all roots of goodness;
the mind that awakens to all Buddha-dharmas. These are the four.
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to four kinds of mountain-like minds.
What are these four? They are:
a mind free from anger or disdain toward those who beg;..."
A mind of compassion and pity toward those heading for the evil realms;
a mind that never abandons the *prajñāpāramitā*;
and a mind that brings all practiced deeds to ultimate completion.
These are the four.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to four kinds of increasingly superior resolve. What are these four?
That is to say: the excellence of upholding the precepts;
the excellence of extensive learning;
and the excellence of great loving-kindness.
Great compassion becomes increasingly superior; these are the four.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to four kinds of adamantine, indestructible minds.
What are the four? They are:
being unshakable in faith and aspiration;
and being unshakable in reliance upon virtuous friends.
The non-destruction of spiritual practice;
the non-destruction of seeking the Mahāyāna. These are the four.
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to four kinds of minds that cannot be defiled.
What are these four? They are:
the mind that afflictions cannot defile;..."
They cannot be defiled by fame or profit;
they cannot be defiled by the Lesser Vehicle;
they cannot be defiled by evil sentient beings.
These are the four.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should give rise to four kinds of unsurpassed resolve. What are these four?
That is to say: the mind that relinquishes all that is beloved;
the mind free from regret after having given;
and the mind that does not look for karmic retribution.
Dedicating [merit] toward the mind of enlightenment—
these are the four. Furthermore, there are four kinds of dharmas by which a bodhisattva can reach the summit.
What are the four? They are: wisdom; skillful means;
Upholding the true Dharma;
transforming sentient beings.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of paths that assist the bodhi of a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
diligently practicing the various perfections (pāramitās);..."
They accord with the four means of attraction;
they abide in the four Brahma-abodes;
and they sport with the supernormal powers.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of supreme and preeminent dharmas of a bodhisattva. What are the four?
That is to say: having no mind of harm or affliction toward any sentient beings;
having no thoughts of attachment toward those who harm or afflict oneself;
and remaining free from negligence even when amidst the objects of the five desires.
Not abandoning the practice of the Dharma despite poverty and suffering— this is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of peaceful minds for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? When one is a householder, one is content with one's own wealth and does not covet the wealth of others.
When going forth, one relies upon the four noble lineages and practices the dhūta ascetic virtues;
these are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of giving for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
the gift of material wealth;"
The gift of Dharma;
the gift of paper and pens;
and the gift of praising with a virtuous mind toward the Dharma Master.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of firm and superior qualities of a bodhisattva.
What are these four?
That is to say: practicing what one has heard;
being able to give away abundant wealth;
and being able to make offerings to those who are venerable.
"Able to plant all roots of goodness throughout one's lifespan— this is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of non-abandonment for a bodhisattva."
What are the four? They are:
not abandoning the bodhicitta;
not abandoning the true Dharma; [and so forth].
Not abandoning any sentient beings;
not abandoning the pursuit of all wholesome dharmas. These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of gardens for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
delighting in dwelling in an araṇya;..."
They delight in sitting alone in the open air;
they delight in seeking the wholesome Dharma;
and they delight in employing skillful means to deliver all sentient beings.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of palaces for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
They delight in relying on the Brahma-abodes;
they delight in hearing the sublime Dharma;
they delight in contemplating the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
To dwell together with those who share the same practice—
this is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of inexhaustible wealth for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are the wealth of extensive learning; the wealth of teaching the Dharma; [the wealth of generosity; and the wealth of wisdom].
The wealth that gathers for the destitute;
the wealth dedicated toward enlightenment.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of treasuries for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
They are the treasury of dhāraṇīs;..."
The treasury of eloquence;
the treasury of the Dharma;
and the treasury of the dedication of inexhaustible wealth.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of seclusion for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
That is to say: being far removed from worldly chatter;
being far removed from the objects of the five desires;
and being far removed from non-noble states of mind.
To remain far removed from the three realms— this is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of joy for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
the joy of non-attachment through being free from the notions of "I" and "mine";
the joy of detachment through having no lingering attachment to anything; [and so forth].
The joy of tranquility through detachment from all objective spheres;
and the joy of nirvana through being free from affliction while not abandoning any sentient beings.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of joy for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
joy upon seeing the Buddha;..."
The joy of hearing the Dharma;
the joy of giving without regret;
and the joy of bestowing peace and happiness upon all sentient beings.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of reality for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
That is to say: not abandoning the bodhicitta;
not abandoning the great vows;
and not abandoning those who come for refuge.
Not abandoning all well-guarded speech—
this constitutes the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of wholesome dharmas for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
delighting in the cultivation of all wholesome dharmas; not disparaging those who have not yet studied; [and the remaining two].
To regard all sentient beings with equanimity toward both enemies and kin;
to act as an uninvited friend to benefit sentient beings without thinking of a reward—
these are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of purity for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
purity of ethical discipline, because of non-self;..."
Concentration is pure because there are no sentient beings;
wisdom is pure because there is no life-principle;
liberation is pure because there are no births in the various realms of existence.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of feet for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
That is to say: the foot of meaning;
the foot of Dharma;
and the foot of the merit of practicing the dhūtas.
Accumulating the provisions for enlightenment—
these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of hands belonging to a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are the hand of faith; the hand of ethical discipline; [the hand of generosity; and the hand of wisdom].
The hand of hearing and the hand of wisdom— these are the four.
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva has four kinds of eyes.
What are the four? They are the fleshly eye, because of having performed wholesome karma;..."
The divine eye, because its supernormal powers do not regress;
the wisdom eye, because one never tires of what is heard;
the dharma eye, because one attains patience through the contemplative observation of all phenomena.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of tirelessness for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
That is to say: being insatiable in giving;
being insatiable in dwelling in an araṇya;
and being insatiable in listening to the Dharma.
To cultivate virtue without weariness—
this constitutes the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of difficult practices for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
enduring all forms of lowliness and humiliation;
and although one is personally destitute, giving away everything one possesses.
When seeing those who beg for one's head, eyes, or body, one’s mind feels no resistance and conceives of them as virtuous friends;
observing emptiness and non-self, one nevertheless manifests birth.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of health for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
That is to say: there are no diseases caused by the imbalance of the elements;
no diseases of the fever of afflictions;
and no diseases that fail to benefit sentient beings.
To be free from the sickness of doubt regarding all phenomena— this is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of natural dharmas of a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are the various pāramitās and the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharmas).
To rely on true spiritual friends;
and to refrain from committing any unwholesome deeds. These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of immovability for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are as follows: the bodhicitta;"
Acting according to one's vows;
acting as one has spoken;
and diligently cultivating correct practice.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of provisions for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
Namely: śamatha; vipaśyanā; and hearing everything.
These are the four roots of goodness.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of equal practice for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
generating the mind and initiating practice;
and dedicating acts of giving.
Great loving-kindness and great compassion;
wisdom and skillful means— these are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams that indicate obstacles to the Dharma for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
dreaming that the moon falls into a level ground well;"
He dreams that the moon appears in a pool of turbid spring water;
he dreams that the moon in the sky is covered by great clouds;
he dreams that the moon in the sky is obscured by smoke and dust.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dream-obscurations of karma for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
That is to say: dreaming of falling into a great precipice;
dreaming of ascending and descending paths;
dreaming of winding and crooked paths.
Dreaming of being lost in one's direction and feeling terrified; these are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams concerning the obstacle of afflictions for a bodhisattva.
What are the four? They are:
dreaming of being disturbed by a venomous snake;
and dreaming of the evil cries of a pack of wild beasts.
Dreaming of falling into a place of banditry and peril;
dreaming of one’s body being covered in dust and filth. These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams through which a bodhisattva attains dhāraṇīs.
What are the four? They are:
dreaming of a great hidden treasure filled with all manner of jewels;..."
He dreamed that various flowers bloomed together in a clear pond;
he dreamed that he obtained a pair of pure white cotton cloths;
and he dreamed that various devas held parasols to shade him from above.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams through which a bodhisattva attains samādhi. What are the four?
That is to say: dreaming of a beautiful young maiden adorned with various jewels who hands her flowers to him;
dreaming of a flight of white geese soaring and wheeling in the sky;
and dreaming of the Tathāgata’s hand stroking the crown of his head.
He dreams that the Tathāgata is seated upon a lotus throne and has entered into samādhi.
This is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams in which a bodhisattva sees the Tathāgata.
What are the four? They are:
dreaming of the appearance of the moon;
dreaming of the appearance of the sun; [and so forth].
Dreaming of a lotus flower blooming;
dreaming of the Great Brahma King with a serene and tranquil demeanor.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams that a bodhisattva has regarding the marks of a great man.
What are the four? They are:
dreaming that various exquisite flowers and fruits fill the śāla trees;..."
He dreamed that great bronze vessels were filled with various jewels;
he dreamed that the sky was adorned with banners and canopies;
and he dreamed of a wheel-turning monarch ruling the world through the Dharma.
These are the four.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams that are signs of non-retrogression for a bodhisattva. What are the four?
That is to say: dreaming of a white silk ribbon tied around one's head;
dreaming of personally arranging an unimpeded assembly for giving;
and dreaming of one's body seated upon the Dharma throne.
Dreaming of the Buddha sitting at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly—
this is the fourth.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams of the Bodhisattva subduing the enemy Māra.
What are the four? They are:
dreaming that a powerful wrestler crushes a weakling and departs carrying a banner of victory;
and dreaming that a great heroic general emerges victorious from battle and departs.
Dreaming of receiving the royal consecration;
dreaming of sitting beneath the Bodhi tree and subduing the hosts of Māra.
These are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of dreams of the Bodhisattva sitting at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
What are the four? They are:
dreaming of an auspicious vase filled to the brim;..."
He dreamed that a multitude circumambulated his body from the right;
he dreamed that wherever he went, the trees all bent their branches downward;
and he dreamed that golden light shone everywhere.
"These are the four.

When Mañjuśrī spoke this Dharma, the Devaputra Suvikrānta and his retinue rejoiced and leaped for joy; they made offerings of celestial māndārava flowers, padma flowers, kumuda flowers, and puṇḍarīka flowers to Mañjuśrī, scattering them over the entire assembly.
Through the Buddha’s supernatural power, the scattered flowers ascended into the void and formed great lotuses, as large as chariot wheels;
they were exquisite, fragrant, and pure, delighting the hearts of all who beheld them.
Upon the flower pedestals were various bodhisattvas, their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man.
At that time, the Devaputra Suśānta addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"From what direction have these bodhisattvas come?"
Mañjuśrī replied, "As is the place from which the flower comes, that is where it has come from.
The deva said:
"This flower has arisen through transformation; it comes from nowhere.
Mañjuśrī spoke again:
"Those bodhisattvas should know that they are likewise so!"

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled and emitted various rays of light from his mouth—colors such as blue, yellow, red, white, and crystal—which illuminated immeasurable lands throughout the ten directions, reaching upward to the Brahma world and eclipsing the light of the sun and moon, before returning to enter through the crown of his head.
Then the Devaputra Bhadrajaya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and praised him in verse:
“With pure golden light and the thirty-two marks of excellence,
Possessing billions of nayutas of incomparable and supreme virtues.”
O Savior of the World, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
Your Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching; your speech is pure and subtle.
You constantly accumulate the seven treasures of the noble ones and radiate the great light of wisdom.
With a voice like that of the kalaviṅka bird, I pray you explain the meaning of your smile.
O Hero of the World, Great Man, who has subdued Māra and the heterodox teachers,
and who is constantly honored by devas, humans, asuras, and others— please speak.
O You who are endowed with the ten powers, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
Having forever severed all greed, hatred, and delusion, along with the dust of afflictions and the obstacles to wisdom,
leaving no residual habits behind, your face is like the pure, full moon.
O Universal Bestower of Peace and Bliss, please explain the meaning of your smile.
Sugata, Teacher of Gods and Humans, you are a mass of immeasurable merit;
your mind is ever-equal, and you are fully endowed with the practice of all virtues.
O Dispeller of All, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
You constantly hold the great lamp of wisdom to shatter the dense forest of darkness;
your gait is like that of a bull king, and you are as fearless as a lion.
O benefactor of sentient beings, please explain the meaning of your smile.
Most honored and supreme among men, you are difficult to see and difficult to fathom;
free from selfhood and without guile, you have transcended the ocean of all existence.
O Master of Wisdom and Sovereignty, for what reason do you manifest a smile?
With feet marked by wheels of a thousand spokes and webbed fingers, peerless throughout the three realms,
you have dried up the flow of birth and death and severed the net of ignorance.
"Excellent, O Great Wise One! We pray that you will explain the meaning of your smile.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Devaputra Suśreṣṭha, saying:
"Do you see the bodhisattvas upon the lotus thrones in the midst of space?"
The devaputra replied,
“Indeed, I have seen them!
The Buddha said:

"These bodhisattvas have all been transformed and delivered by Mañjuśrī; for the sake of hearing these four Dharma-gates, they have come from the ten directions. They all dwell in the stage of being one birth away from Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in buddha-fields throughout the ten directions, each with a different name."
The deva said:
"World-Honored One!
Is it possible to calculate and know the number of these bodhisattvas?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Śāriputra:
“Are you able to know this? Śāriputra replied:
“World-Honored One!
I am able, in the span of a single thought-moment, to know all the stars within a trichiliocosm; yet I could not calculate the number of these bodhisattvas even in a hundred years!”
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Even if the atoms filling Jambudvīpa could be counted, the number of these bodhisattvas would be beyond the reach of knowledge."
Śāriputra said, “Where could there be so many buddha-fields to accommodate these bodhisattvas attaining perfect enlightenment?
The Buddha said:
"Cease, do not speak thus!
There are immeasurable and boundless worlds in which no Buddha currently dwells. Śāriputra!"
Suppose that the Tathāgata were to remain in the world for as many eons as there are sands in the Ganges, preaching as many teachings each day as there are sands in the Ganges;
and suppose that for each teaching preached, he were to bestow the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* upon as many bodhisattvas as there are sands in the Ganges;
and suppose that beyond as many Buddha-fields to the east as there are sands in the Ganges, only a single bodhisattva would attain Buddhahood therein.
"In this way, even the Buddha-less worlds in the eastern direction cannot be fully exhausted, let alone all the lands throughout the ten directions that are empty and devoid of Buddhas. Śāriputra!"
All such infinite worlds as these are seen by the Tathāgata’s physical eye;
all sentient beings therein are known by the Tathāgata’s mind.
At that time, the great śrāvakas and the entire assembly were filled with wonder and spoke thus:
"We have all now attained a sublime benefit, having encountered such a teacher who has accomplished such vast merit and wisdom!"

At that time, all the bodhisattvas who had come from throughout the void descended from the sky, prostrated themselves before the Tathāgata and Mañjuśrī, circumambulated them respectfully to the right, and each returned to their own native land.
At that time, the Devaputra Suvikrānta addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Excellent, O Venerable One!
You perform the work of a Buddha, for you are able to transform these immeasurable bodhisattvas so that they abide in great enlightenment."
“I pray that you will explain to me how these dharmas for abiding in enlightenment are accomplished. Mañjuśrī said, “O Devaputra!
There are thirty-five factors for accomplishing the bodhisattva’s dwelling in the dharma of enlightenment: namely, one should always rely on the proper time without missing its season;
one should vigilantly restrain the sense faculties;
and one should collect the mind so that it does not waver.
One should cultivate the various pāramitās;
one should follow skillful means;
and one should generate the superior intention.
One should establish great loving-kindness;
one should give rise to great compassion;
one should not abandon the Mahāyāna.
One should distance oneself from the Lesser Vehicle;
one should always be truthful and sincere;
and one should act according to reality.
One should protect the true Dharma;
one should practice according to what has been heard;
and one should understand that the nature of sentient beings is equal and non-dual.
One should contemplate that both the breaking and the upholding of precepts are the marks of a field of merit;
one should awaken to all demonic activities;
and one should bring great vows to full completion.
One should not grow weary or disheartened within the cycle of birth and death;
one should subdue all Māras;
and one should recognize kindness and repay it.
One should enter into the dharmas that cause cessation;
one should not be terrified by the gates of liberation;
and one should make offerings to all Buddhas.
One should act for the sake of all according to the needs of sentient beings;
one should remain unstained by worldly dharmas;
and one should delight in the forest hermitage (āraṇya).
One should practice fewness of desires;
one should maintain mindfulness of contentment;
and one should cause those who have not yet crossed over to cross over.
Those who have not yet understood, one should cause them to understand;
those who have not yet attained peace, one should cause them to attain peace;
those who have not yet attained nirvana, one should cause them to attain nirvana.
One should not sever the lineage of the Three Jewels;
one should encompass the meritorious adornments of the pure lands of all Buddhas.
These constitute the thirty-five dharmas for a bodhisattva’s dwelling in enlightenment, and one should train accordingly.
"Furthermore, O Devaputra!
A bodhisattva should abandon ten kinds of conceit, namely: the conceit of 'I am' (asmimāna); the conceit of being learned (bahuśrutamāna);..."
Arrogance regarding eloquence;
arrogance regarding gain, offerings, and reputation;
arrogance regarding dwelling in an araṇya.
Pride in the merits of dhūta practices;
pride in wealth, status, and retinue;
pride in being served by Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors.
The pride of meditative concentration and supernormal powers;
and the pride of receiving the unshakable faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and being reverently praised by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others.
If a bodhisattva can abandon these ten kinds of pride, they will not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and will not be defeated by any heterodox teachers, Māras, or adversaries.
Then the Devaputra Suśānta addressed Mañjuśrī, saying:
“Wherever the Venerable One dwells, it should be known that this Dharma-gate already exists there; it is as if the Tathāgata has appeared in that place to turn the wheel of the true Dharma.”
The Buddha said: "So it is, so it is!
It is just as you have said."
In whichever direction or land Mañjuśrī preaches this Dharma-gate, he dwells therein as a King of the Dharma.
Any sentient beings who practice this Dharma are true sons of the Buddha.

Those who are able to believe, understand, receive, and uphold this Dharma are called true practitioners; such persons have been tamed by the Buddha and shall not regress from Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, Kāśyapa, and Ānanda:
“Sons of good family!
I now entrust this Dharma-gate to you; you should receive, uphold, read, recite, practice it according to the teaching, and explain it extensively for others.”
"After my parinirvāṇa, you should perform great Buddha-work with this Dharma, so that all sentient beings may attain peace and happiness.
Maitreya replied, "So be it;
I shall receive these instructions!"
"Bhagavān, what should this sutra be named?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:
“This sutra is titled ‘The Exposition of the Four Dharma-Gates,’ and it is also titled ‘The Method for Accomplishing the Bodhisattva Path. Therefore, you all should together receive and uphold it.”

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, the Elder Mahākāśyapa, the Elder Ānanda, and all the world’s devas, humans, asuras, and others, having heard what the Buddha taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Four Dharmas
